name: Blepharoplasty

lead: Blepharoplasty is the standard operation for droopy upper lids and lower-lid bags, removing or repositioning skin, muscle and fat. Surgeons also perform it to improve vision when lids obstruct sight, and East Asian double-eyelid surgery is one of the most common variants.

Looksmaxxing members discuss it for eye shape, ptosis and tiredness, usually combined with fat grafts or brow work. Surgical literature supports it for dermatochalasis and bags; claims about dramatic eye-shape changes are mainly forum accounts.

paras: Incisions in the lid crease (upper) or beneath the lashes or inside the lid (lower) allow removal, repositioning or preservation of skin, muscle and fat. Canthal support may be added to stabilise the lower lid.

Swelling and bruising are common for weeks; dry eye, lid malposition and asymmetry are reported complications, and a 1987 infection cluster was traced to contaminated skin-marking solution. Surgeons often combine it with canthal support to reduce malposition.

lead: Blepharoplasty, commonly called eyelid surgery, is plastic surgery that removes or repositions excess skin, muscle and fat of the upper or lower eyelids. It is performed for functional reasons, such as heavy upper lids that reduce peripheral vision, and for cosmetic reasons, such as reducing hooding or under-eye bags.[1][2][3]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a hardmaxxing option for the eye area, often alongside fat grafting, brow repositioning or canthal procedures, and members debate whether it would improve eye shape, ptosis, or perceived tiredness.[4][5][6]

Reviews describe upper blepharoplasty as having both aesthetic and functional outcomes, and a 2023 systematic review compared techniques and outcomes including effects on the cornea, intraocular pressure, dry eye and visual quality.[2] A 2026 review characterised modern practice as having shifted from subtractive techniques toward tissue preservation and augmentation.[7] Wikipedia notes the procedure is more common in women (about 85% of US cases in 2014) and that Asian (double-eyelid) blepharoplasty is among the most common procedures in several East Asian countries.[1]
infobox: Upper, lower (transcutaneous or transconjunctival), Asian double-eyelid
Canthopexy/canthoplasty, fat repositioning or grafting, midface lift
Swelling and bruising usually fade over several weeks

paras: Upper blepharoplasty uses an incision in the natural eyelid crease to remove or reposition skin, muscle and sometimes fat. Lower blepharoplasty can be transcutaneous (incision beneath the lashes) or transconjunctival (inside the lid, leaving no external scar, but not removing skin).[1][3]

Contemporary lower blepharoplasty increasingly includes relocating orbital fat to correct inferior orbital hollowing, tear trough deformity and lid-cheek junction effacement rather than only removing fat.[3] An older paper on arcus marginalis release and orbital fat preservation argued that conventional fat removal can create a concave contour deformity.[8]
Newer variants include pinch blepharoplasty for the lower lid and office-based approaches.[9] Surgeons may add canthopexy or canthoplasty to support the lower lid.[1]

Excess upper-lid skin can drape over the lashes and reduce the visual field, making driving and reading harder; lower-lid indications include excess skin, weakened septum, fat bulging and malposition.[1]

People seek surgery to reduce under-eye bags or upper-lid hooding associated with ageing.[1] East Asian double-eyelid surgery creates or raises a supratarsal fold; one study describes a three-mini-incision technique for this purpose.[10][1]

The 2023 meta-analysis of upper blepharoplasty techniques examined surgical technique and aesthetic and functional outcomes.[2] A registered study is evaluating patient-reported outcomes with the FACE-Q instrument in blepharoplasty,[11] and others are assessing functional changes and vision quality after upper blepharoplasty.[12][13]
Wikipedia reports typical results as smoother lid contours and a more defined lid-cheek junction, varying with anatomy and technique.[1]

Swelling and bruising are common and usually resolve in weeks.[1] A randomised trial examined compression dressings after upper blepharoplasty for edema, ecchymosis, pain and ocular surface irritation.[14] Reviews describe dry eye and effects on ocular surface and cornea as outcomes assessed after upper blepharoplasty,[2] and lower lid malposition, scleral show and ectropion as complications of lower-lid surgery that canthal support aims to reduce.[3][1]
In 1987 a cluster of Mycobacterium chelonae wound infections after plastic surgery was traced to a contaminated gentian violet skin-marking solution.[15]

Greek and Roman physicians recorded eyelid techniques; Celsus described cutting the skin to relax the lids in the first century. Karl Ferdinand von Graefe coined the term blepharoplasty in 1818 while describing repairs of eyelid deformities after cancer.[1]

Human evidence includes a systematic review and meta-analysis of upper blepharoplasty,[2] randomised trials of compression dressings after upper blepharoplasty[14] and of lower eyelid blepharoplasty outcomes and satisfaction, case series of mini-incision double-eyelid technique,[10] and non-surgical alternatives such as microplasma for dermatochalasis, a clinical trial.[16] Registered studies address FACE-Q outcomes, functional changes, vision quality and fat preservation.[11][12][13][17]

On looksmax.org, members ask whether upper and lower blepharoplasty with fat grafts would 'ascend' the eye area, and some repliers suggest brow repositioning as an alternative.[4] Others discuss whether surgery would resolve ptosis-related asymmetry when the eyeballs or orbits themselves appear asymmetric.[5] Members also list blepharoplasty among multiple procedures in before-and-after posts.[6]

lore.intro: Blepharoplasty is discussed on looksmax.org as a way to change eyelid appearance and as one element of multi-procedure eye-area plans.[4][5][6]
